1:
Nobody here reads the division as a map. Gill says the land was never so divided among the twelve tribes literally, neither in Joshua's time nor after the captivity of Babylon, and takes the whole for the Christian church; the stranger sojourners promised a share in the previous chapter are not named, though included, being Israelites indeed and fellowheirs. Henry reaches the same conclusion from the details: the arrangement agrees neither with the order of the tribes' birth nor with the blessings of Jacob or of Moses, since Simeon is not divided here and Zebulun is no haven of ships, a plain intimation that the passage is to be understood spiritually, though he grants the mystery of it is very much hidden. He notices too how brief the procedure is, since in the distribution of spiritual blessings there is not the danger of murmuring that attends temporal ones. Clarke sends the reader to the older border list in the law as casting much light on it.

The order of the names is where Henry finds most to say. Dan, last provided for in the first division of Canaan, comes first here, and lies furthest of all from the sanctuary, because that tribe had revolted to idolatry. Reuben, whose lot had formerly lain beyond Jordan, now lies next to Judah and next but one to the sanctuary, the scandal he lay under having begun to wear off; what has turned to the reproach of any person or people, Henry remarks, ought not to be remembered for ever. He observes too that the ten tribes carried away by Assyria are allotted portions here along with the two that went to Babylon.

Gill takes each name as a description of a class of believer. Naphtali stands for those who wrestle with God in prayer and contend for the doctrines of the Gospel, Manasseh for those who forget what is behind, their former companions and their own righteousness, Reuben for those who look to the Son, and Judah for those who confess the Lord and praise his name. He notes that Joseph is not named because his two portions go to his sons, and that Manasseh is now a whole tribe with an inheritance equal to the rest.

That the lots touch one another is pressed by both. Gill makes the contiguity a figure of the union of believers, and looks to the latter day when they shall no more grieve and vex each other. Henry puts it as a piece of building: by the border of one tribe lay the portion of another, all in a row and in exact order, so that like stones in an arch they wedged in one another. He adds that the sanctuary stands in the midst, seven tribes north of it and the rest to the south, so that it lies in the heart of the kingdom.

The reserved portion draws the closest reading. Clarke gives its measure and says the temple stood in the centre, the whole being destined for the priests, the Levites and the prince. Keil and Delitzsch renders it not an offering but a heave lifted off, reckons the breadth in rods where the received version has reeds, and supplies tribe-lot where the Hebrew leaves only the numeral. Gill says the priests' share is to build houses on and hold as most holy, and remarks that simony is not to be practised. Ellicott notes two changes from the older law: the Levites receive a portion the same size as the priests', instead of nearly three times as many cities, and the rule forbidding even a temporary alienation of the fields about their cities is extended to their whole land, on the express ground that it is firstfruits. Henry adds why the share fell to the sons of Zadok, who went not astray when Israel and the other Levites went astray.
15:
What is left after the priests and Levites have been served is common ground, and the voices agree on the arithmetic but differ on the unit. Gill counts reeds. Keil and Delitzsch counts in rods, and works out that when ten thousand of breadth have been measured off for the priests and ten thousand for the Levites, five thousand remain along the long side, to be common and not holy land for the city, part for dwelling-houses and part for the open precinct, with the city in the centre of the oblong. Ellicott explains the word profane as marking a contrast, not a defect, since this strip stands over against the holy possession of the Levites and the most holy portion of the priests, though still part of the oblation. Wesley says the same in five words, a common and not a consecrated place.

Clarke reckons in cubits instead, and gets from the remainder a second city where laymen might dwell who served the priests and Levites lodging in the temple, and a strip for fields and gardens to support them. He remarks that on this reckoning there was no cultivated land between the Levites and the prince except on the east and west sides. Wesley states the disagreement outright, giving the city's content in cubits and adding that they are not reeds. Keil and Delitzsch treats one of the figures for the city as corrupt, a word having crept in through a copyist's error and marked by the Masoretes as written but not to be read.

On the shape of the city there is no dispute. Ellicott makes it an exact square with an open space on all four sides, the whole coming to a square whose side is a little under ten miles, exactly the width of what was left of the oblation. Keil and Delitzsch adds that the city with its precinct therefore filled the entire breadth left over.

Who serves the city and how it is fed is read morally by one and structurally by another. Gill takes the servants for magistrates and ministers alike, drawn out of the several tribes, so that all have the honour as well as the labour of serving the church. Ellicott makes the point institutional: the city belongs to no particular tribe but stands on the common oblation, its labourers taken alike from all, so that the old jealousies are extinguished and each tribe treated like every other. On the field set apart for their food he registers a difficulty rather than solving it, since a piece of land only four times the size of the city would seem a very insufficient provision for its labourers; here, as everywhere, the description is to be remembered as ideal. Wesley notes only that it maintains the city officers.

The prince's portion brings that judgment to a head. Gill takes the prince for no magistrate but the Prince Messiah, King and Protector of his people. Clarke places it alongside the Levites', running west to east and equal above and below. Ellicott first untangles the wording, which he calls obscure from its brevity and want of punctuation, giving the prince whatever is left of the oblation between it and the tribal portions; and then denies that anything can be calculated from it. On the estimate of the cubit he has adopted the arrangement is geographically impossible, and even at eighteen inches, the smallest estimate that can well be made, the side of the oblation would still exceed the distance between the Jordan and the Mediterranean at its northern end. It is quite idle, he concludes, to attempt any calculation of the prince's portion. He will not save the figures by supposing the measures to follow the uneven ground and the sinuosities of the roads, since that at once destroys all possibility of following them, and is opposed to the whole symmetry of the description.
23:
The southern half of the division is handled briefly, and Ellicott says why: the remaining five tribes have their portions assigned on the south of the oblation in precisely the same way as the seven on the north, so that nothing new is introduced. Gill marks the same symmetry from the other end, noting that the description begins at the northern part of the land and ends in the southern.

Gill continues here the reading he began in the northern tribes, taking each name for a class of believer. Simeon stands for those who hear, understand and believe the Gospel, and practise what they hear; and he observes that this tribe is no longer divided and scattered in Israel, nor given its inheritance inside the portion of Judah as it was formerly, but stands distinct with a portion of its own. Issachar stands for those who receive the rewards of grace for their services and their sufferings in times of tribulation. Zebulun, who is here no more a haven for ships, having a different situation altogether, stands for those who dwell in Christ and in whom he dwells. Gad, the last of them, stands for a troop of overcomers, who are more than conquerors over all their enemies. The series closes with the general application, that all Christians shall have their part and portion in the church below, in all its privileges, and in the church above, in all its blessedness.

Clarke leaves the moral reading alone and fixes the southern boundary on the ground. Tamar he places on the south of the Dead Sea, and Kadesh, or Kadesh-Barnea, still farther south, at the extremity of the portion of Gad; and he points out the symmetry of the two ends, Gad being the most southern of the tribes as Dan was the most northern.

On the closing verse, which directs that the land be divided by lot, Gill returns to the point he made at the beginning of the chapter. The inheritance described is not of a worldly but of a spiritual nature, and those who receive it are the Israelites indeed; the goodly heritage promised is a place in the house and church of God, with a right to enjoy all the ordinances of it, and he calls it a place and a name better than sons and daughters.
30:
The closing measurement produces the widest disagreement in the chapter, because nobody knows what unit is meant. Henry states the problem squarely: it is never said in all this chapter whether the numbers are so many reeds, as the English translation determines by inserting that word, or so many cubits; and those who take them for cubits are not agreed whether the common cubit, half a yard, or the longer measure used in surveying land, is meant. He turns the uncertainty into the lesson, that being left at a loss is an intimation that these things are to be understood spiritually, and that what is meant is the exact proportion observed by Infinite Wisdom in the gospel church, which we cannot discern now but shall in heaven. The results bear him out. Ellicott makes the circuit, not counting the open space, something over thirty-four miles, and sets beside it the reckoning of Josephus, who put Jerusalem's circuit in his own day at four. Wesley makes the same number five miles in compass. Gill cites a reckoning that makes it thirty-two thousand, and takes the absurdity as proof that no literal city can be meant, but the church spread over the world; he adds that certain Jewish writers, not knowing what to make of such measures, referred them to the eighteen thousand worlds God is said to have made. Clarke keeps to cubits and totals the sides.

The gates are the point of the repetition. Ellicott says the dimensions are given a second time in order to introduce them, three on each side, one for each tribe; Levi here takes his place as a tribe, so that Joseph is reckoned as only one, and the order of the names follows neither their geographical arrangement nor their seniority. Henry accounts for the same adjustment from the other end, Levi being taken in and Ephraim and Manasseh made one in Joseph to keep the number at twelve; and he thinks it fit each tribe should have its gate, the city being served out of all the tribes. Gill reads the inscribed names as a title of entrance, showing that all true Israelites have a right of access; and he adds that the gates, twelve with respect to the tribes and the apostles, are in the main but one, which is Christ.

The name given at the end carries the weight of the whole vision. Henry observes first what is absent: the city is nowhere called Jerusalem, nor the land anywhere the land of Canaan, the old names being dropped to intimate that old things are done away; and the name given is not the vision of peace but the thing behind it, that the Lord is there. Clarke would have kept the Hebrew words untranslated, and reads them as an allusion to the visible sign of the divine presence which stood in the first temple and most certainly not in the second. Wesley draws the inference that this presence makes us happy and its withdrawal leaves us to misery, and that a believer may write the name over any place where he stands in his duty. Ellicott calls it a most fitting close, the object throughout having been to depict, under the figures of the older dispensation, the glories of the Church to come.

Clarke ends by holding two things together: the prophet meant that when the people were restored they should build the temple and divide the land as directed here, if it could be found practicable, and he had at the same time another temple, another city and another promised land in view. Of the book itself he says that few of the prophets have left a more valuable treasure, and that he has himself passed slightly over the symbols he did not fully understand, leaving it to time to show with what wisdom this much neglected prophet has spoken.
